strengths: The core idea—reformulating standard SSL pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch position) as verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training—is a clean and practical way to avoid human preference data or LLM-as-judge signals, and is a useful reframing even though the underlying tasks are well known.

Broad empirical coverage: vision-centric (ImageNet) and vision-language reasoning (MMBench, SEED-Bench) benchmarks at two model scales (3B/7B), plus a genuinely distinct extension to graph-structured data with three SSL tasks, showing the framework is not narrowly tailored to one modality.

Systematic ablations on task difficulty, model-size scaling, and task combination provide some actionable design heuristics ("difficulty must match model capacity", non-additivity of naively combined rewards) that could be useful starting points for follow-up work.

Reasonably transparent reporting: full per-dimension results in the appendix, training curves, and qualitative case studies (attention maps, example transcripts) that attempt to explain why gains occur (sharper visual grounding, reduced linguistic-prior reliance).
Reproducibility details (hyperparameters, GRPO configuration, evaluation toolkit) are provided, and the authors commit to releasing code.
weaknesses: Missing critical control experiments: there is no baseline that applies GRPO/RL with a verifiable but semantically irrelevant reward (e.g., arbitrary classification or formatting-compliance reward) to isolate whether gains stem from SSL task semantics specifically or simply from generic RL post-training that improves instruction-following/output formatting on multiple-choice benchmarks. Given the very large jumps reported (e.g., +39 points on MMBench Relation Reasoning from a rotation-prediction reward), this confound is plausible and not ruled out.

The mechanistic explanations offered (e.g., rotation prediction as "anti-commonsense learning," contrastive task "too easy" hence weak) are post-hoc narratives supported mainly by 2-3 qualitative attention-map examples rather than systematic, quantitative evidence (e.g., attention entropy/IoU statistics across a larger sample, ablations directly testing the causal claims).

No variance/robustness reporting: single-run numbers are given throughout without seeds, error bars, or statistical significance testing, which is important given how large and sometimes non-monotonic (e.g., task combination underperforming best single task) the reported effects are.

The task-combination experiment shows no improvement over single-task training, weakening the generality/robustness narrative, and the explanation for this remains speculative without further diagnostic experiments (e.g., examining gradient conflict directly).
Minor inconsistencies between reported average improvements in the abstract (9%/8%) and in the main text (7.39%/8.94%) suggest limited care in number reporting, which raises reproducibility concerns.

The graph extension applies a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) to text-attributed graph tasks without clear justification of why a vision-language model (rather than a text-only LLM or a GNN) is the appropriate backbone for this domain, making the "generalization to graph" claim somewhat orthogonal to the paper's main vision-language motivation and harder to interpret.

No comparison to alternative post-training baselines (e.g., RLHF/DPO with human/AI preference data, or straightforward SFT/RL directly on downstream VQA data) that would contextualize how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific SSL-derived rewards versus simply doing additional RL fine-tuning at all.

Limited discussion of reward hacking or degenerate solutions in the SSL4RL rewards (e.g., models exploiting superficial cues to solve rotation/jigsaw without learning transferable visual grounding), despite this being a central risk in reward-shaping approaches.

strengths: The central idea—reframing SSL pretext objectives (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch position) as verifiable rewards for GRPO-based RL post-training of VLMs—is a reasonable and relatively underexplored way to avoid human preference data or LLM-as-judge rewards.

The empirical study is reasonably broad: two model scales (3B/7B), two vision-language reasoning benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench), a vision-centric benchmark (ImageNet), and an extension to graph learning, together with ablations on task difficulty, model size, and task combination.
The qualitative analyses (attention-map visualizations, case studies on language-prior reliance) provide some intuitive support for the claim that SSL4RL sharpens visual grounding.

The negative results reported honestly (e.g., non-additivity of combined SSL rewards, diminishing returns with larger model size, contrastive learning underperforming without stronger augmentation) show a degree of scientific candor rather than only presenting favorable outcomes.
Detailed appendix with task prompts, per-category results, and reward curves aids transparency of what was actually run.
weaknesses: No baseline isolates whether gains are specifically attributable to SSL-derived rewards versus simply performing additional GRPO fine-tuning with any verifiable, structured-output reward (e.g., a control task unrelated to SSL, or a simple SFT baseline on the same SSL targets). Without such controls, the paper cannot support its central causal claim that self-supervision specifically (rather than generic RL post-training with CoT-formatted verifiable answers) drives the improvements.

No variance/seed analysis is reported despite RL training being known to be unstable; single-run numbers (some improvements exceeding 30-39 percentage points) are reported without confidence intervals or repeated trials, undermining reliability of the claimed gains.

Potential format/overfitting confound is not examined: SSL4RL training enforces a strict <think>/<answer> CoT output format; MMBench/SEED-Bench are multiple-choice benchmarks evaluated via VLMEvalKit, and the paper does not verify that gains reflect genuine visual grounding rather than improved answer-formatting/extraction compliance from RL training itself.

No comparison against existing RL-for-VLM baselines (e.g., standard RLHF, DPO, or LLM-as-judge RL) that the paper explicitly motivates against in Sections 1–2; without any such comparison, it is impossible to assess whether SSL4RL is competitive with, better than, or worse than alternatives it claims to improve upon.

Source and provenance of images used for SSL4RL training are not specified, leaving open the possibility of overlap/contamination with MMBench/SEED-Bench/ImageNet test images, which is not discussed or controlled for.

The graph-domain extension is under-specified: it is unclear how graph structure/text is fed into a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL), what constitutes the 'image' input if any, and how comparable this setup is to the vision experiments; this weakens the claimed generality of the framework.

Several post-hoc explanations (e.g., rotation as 'anti-commonsense learning', jigsaw over-specialization at higher difficulty) are speculative narrative interpretations not tested by further targeted ablations or statistical analysis.

The qualitative case studies (Figure 3, Figure 8, Figure 9) appear cherry-picked, with no systematic/quantitative measure of hallucination reduction, grounding improvement, or shortcut-reliance decrease across the full evaluation set.
Reward-hacking risks (e.g., models learning to game format-based exact-match discrete rewards without genuinely solving the underlying pretext task) are not discussed or empirically ruled out.

Generalization is confined entirely to a single model family (Qwen2.5-VL) at two scales; no results on other VLM architectures are provided to substantiate broader claims about the paradigm's versatility.

strengths: The core idea—reformulating classic SSL pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch-position) as verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training—is a clean, well-motivated bridge between the SSL and verifiable-reward RL literatures, addressing a real gap (lack of reliable, scalable reward signals outside math/code domains).

The empirical study is broad: two vision-language reasoning benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench), a vision-centric benchmark (ImageNet-1K with three difficulty tiers), and an extension to graph learning with three distinct SSL tasks, showing the framework is not narrowly tied to one modality.

The ablation studies (task difficulty scaling, model size scaling from 3B to 7B, task combination) are thoughtfully designed and yield non-trivial, sometimes counter-intuitive findings (e.g., harder tasks help Contrastive but hurt Jigsaw/Rotation; naive reward combination doesn't help), giving the paper genuine analytical value beyond a single positive result.

Qualitative analyses (attention heatmaps, case studies of reduced linguistic-prior reliance) provide complementary, if informal, evidence that the mechanism of improvement is plausible (sharper visual grounding) rather than purely benchmark-specific overfitting.
Reasonable transparency about hyperparameters, training setup (GRPO configuration, compute), and a stated intent to release code supports reproducibility of the core pipeline.
weaknesses: A major unaddressed confound: SSL4RL-trained models are explicitly optimized to produce structured <think>/<answer> outputs during RL, while the reported 'Base' model numbers appear to come from the off-the-shelf model without this same structured prompting/training. Part of the very large reported gains (e.g., +39pp on MMBench Relation Reasoning, +21pp on SEED TU) could stem from improved answer-extraction/format compliance under VLMEvalKit rather than genuine visual grounding improvements; no ablation isolates format effects from content effects (e.g., an SFT-only or degenerate-reward RL baseline with the same output format is missing).

No comparison against natural alternative baselines that would contextualize the value of SSL-derived rewards, e.g., RL directly on a small labeled subset of the downstream task (an upper bound), RL with random/trivial reward (a lower bound to check if gains are just from RL exploration/regularization), or existing self-reward baselines mentioned in related work (STaR, Self-Consistency, RPT). Without these, it is hard to assess how much of the benefit is specifically attributable to the SSL semantics versus generic RL fine-tuning effects.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere; given the well-known instability of RL training (also visible in the noisy reward curves in Appendix D), single-run point estimates for often large claimed improvements reduce confidence in the statistical robustness of the results.

The explanations for why certain tasks work (e.g., the 'anti-commonsense learning' account for Rotation's effectiveness) are speculative narratives without direct empirical validation (e.g., targeted probing or ablations that isolate this proposed mechanism).

Generalization is only demonstrated on the Qwen2.5-VL family (3B/7B); it remains unclear whether findings (e.g., which SSL task works best, the difficulty-capacity matching principle) transfer to other VLM architectures or training stacks.

The task-combination experiment shows no additive benefit and sometimes underperforms the best single task, which undercuts the paper's framing of SSL4RL as an easily extensible 'recipe'—the practical guidance is limited to picking one well-matched task via trial and error, which is only lightly formalized.

Design principles offered ('task difficulty', 'model scale', 'semantic alignment') are stated somewhat post hoc from a small set of four vision tasks and three graph tasks; the paper does not propose or test a predictive rule that would let a practitioner select/tune an SSL4RL task a priori for a new setting.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical study: the paper evaluates SSL4RL across many benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet-1K, V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite, CapArena), two model families (Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma3) at two scales (3B/7B), and even extends the idea to graph learning with three SSL tasks—providing a comprehensive picture of when the paradigm helps.

The core idea—reformulating self-supervised pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch position) as intrinsically verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training—is a clean, practically useful contribution that avoids reliance on human preference data or LLM-as-judge signals for most of the training pipeline.

Extensive and thoughtful ablations (data volume scaling, model size scaling, task difficulty scaling, task combination, base model choice, robustness to perturbations) go beyond a single positive result and try to extract general design principles ('Goldilocks difficulty', capacity-task alignment, non-additivity of combined rewards).

The comparison against an oracle 'Golden-3B' baseline trained with task-specific golden-answer rewards is a valuable and rigorous way to contextualize how much of the achievable gain SSL4RL can capture without labels.

Qualitative analyses (attention heatmaps, case studies showing reduced reliance on linguistic priors) provide some mechanistic insight into why the method helps, complementing the quantitative results.

The paper is transparent about negative/mixed findings (e.g., contrastive learning underperforming without stronger augmentation, diminishing returns at 7B scale, non-additive task combination), which strengthens the credibility of the analysis rather than only reporting favorable results.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to acknowledged concurrent/prior work (Jigsaw-R1, Spatial-SSRL): the paper's core mechanism (corrupt image, get verifiable reward, apply GRPO) is essentially a generalization of ideas already published, and the paper does not provide a head-to-head quantitative comparison against these closely related methods.

Reported gains are very large in places (e.g., +39 points on MMBench Relation Reasoning, near-chance base-model accuracy on seemingly simple rotation prediction), which raises questions about whether the base-model baseline evaluation (prompting/parsing, zero-shot instruction format) is fully fair, especially since these effects are not cross-validated with alternative baselines or multiple seeds/runs; no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-trial statistics are reported anywhere in the paper.

The open-ended captioning evaluation relies on GPT-4o as a judge (CapArena), which is philosophically in tension with the paper's stated motivation of avoiding 'unreliable AI evaluators'; results in this section are also somewhat noisy/non-monotonic (e.g., Position task gives 0.00 GPT-Score in two of the settings, underperforming even the base model on that sub-metric), undermining the claimed generality of the approach for open-ended tasks.

Model-size scaling study is based on only two points (3B and 7B) plus a single alternative architecture (Gemma3-4B) at reduced batch size, which is a fairly narrow basis for the strong claims made about a general 'capacity-task difficulty matching' principle and 'diminishing returns' trend.

All experiments use an identical fixed GRPO configuration across very different SSL tasks and domains (vision, graph); it is unclear whether this represents a fair comparison, since different reward structures (e.g., binary contrastive vs. multi-class rotation) may need different learning rates, KL coefficients, or group sizes to reach their full potential, potentially confounding the difficulty/task-comparison conclusions.

Several explanatory narratives (e.g., rotation prediction as 'anti-commonsense learning', qualitative attention-sharpening claims) are plausible but only supported by a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples rather than systematic, quantitative validation.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract references an empty code/model URL, and some appendix tables (e.g., graph 7B results, CapArena scores) show non-monotonic or counterintuitive patterns that are not fully discussed or reconciled with the main narrative.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and practically relevant question: how to obtain verifiable, scalable RL reward signals for VLMs without human preference labels or LLM-judges.

Breadth of empirical investigation is substantial: four SSL pretext tasks evaluated across multiple benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite, ImageNet, CapArena), two model sizes (3B/7B), two architectures (Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma3), and an additional domain (graphs), which gives the work a broad empirical footprint.

The ablations on data volume, task difficulty, model size, and task combination are a reasonable attempt to extract design principles, and the paper is commendably candid about negative/counterintuitive findings (e.g., non-additivity of combined SSL rewards, diminishing returns at 7B).
Qualitative analyses (attention maps, example captions) provide some intuitive support for the claimed mechanism of improved visual grounding.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage/overfitting concern: the SSL4RL training data for the main reasoning benchmarks is explicitly drawn from MMBench and SEED-Bench images themselves (Section 4.5.1: 'Base Set: ~4,000 samples from MMBench', 'Extended Set... MMBench and SEED-Bench'), and the model is then evaluated on those same benchmarks. Even though the SSL label (e.g., rotation angle) differs from the benchmark's QA label, training on the exact test-time image distribution (and likely overlapping images) confounds whether gains reflect genuine reasoning improvement or benchmark-specific visual memorization/distribution matching. This is never addressed or controlled for (e.g., no held-out image set, no train/test image split check).

Some reported gains are implausibly large for simple pretext tasks with no semantic relation to the benchmark content — e.g., +39 points on MMBench 'Relation Reasoning' from training on 4-way image rotation prediction. The paper's explanation ('anti-commonsense learning') is speculative narrative rather than mechanistic evidence, and no controlled ablation isolates this causal story from simpler explanations (e.g., leakage, prompt-format effects, or entropy/KL-driven behavior changes shown in Appendix K).

Internal inconsistency: the paper motivates SSL4RL partly by criticizing LLM-as-a-judge as 'biased, noisy, and prone to adversarial manipulation' (Introduction, Related Work), yet the headline open-ended captioning result (CapArena, Section 4.2) relies entirely on GPT-4o as judge — the very mechanism the paper argues against — undermining the claimed contribution in the open-ended setting.

No variance/seed information is reported anywhere (single run per configuration across dozens of tables), making it impossible to assess whether the often large swings between tasks/difficulties (e.g., Contrastive task going from harmful to highly beneficial just by changing augmentation strength) reflect real effects or training noise/instability, especially given RL training is known to be high-variance.

Missing essential baselines/sanity checks: there is no ablation showing performance under (a) RL with a random/uninformative reward, (b) pure SFT with GRPO-style KL regularization but trivial reward, or (c) plain continued pretraining without RL, to isolate how much of the gain is attributable to the SSL reward signal specifically versus general effects of RL fine-tuning, entropy dynamics, or exposure to in-domain images.

The 'unified framework' narrative is weakened by the paper's own findings: task effectiveness is inconsistent across domains (Contrastive hurts on VQA but helps on ImageNet and graph), the four tasks do not combine additively, and model-size scaling yields diminishing/negative returns at 7B — collectively suggesting the method is a set of disconnected, task- and benchmark-specific heuristics rather than a principled, generalizable recipe, which undercuts the claimed significance and the 'design principles for future work.'

The graph extension (Section 5) is thin and underspecified: there is minimal methodological detail on how text-attributed graphs are fed into a VLM, no clarity on architecture adaptation, and results are presented with the same lack of variance/robustness analysis as the vision experiments.

The claimed novelty is modest: the paper explicitly identifies Jigsaw-R1 as highly related prior work using essentially the same core idea (pretext task as RL reward for MLLMs); the contribution here is largely an empirical generalization/sweep rather than a new mechanism, which is a reasonable but limited contribution that the paper oversells as a general 'framework' and 'paradigm.'

Analysis sections rely heavily on post-hoc, qualitative storytelling (e.g., 'fostering integrated spatial understanding,' 'anti-commonsense learning,' 'Goldilocks principle') without quantitative tests that would distinguish these explanations from alternative hypotheses, reducing confidence in the stated design principles.

strengths: Clear and timely idea: reframing self-supervised pretext tasks (rotation, jigsaw, contrastive, patch-position) as verifiable RL rewards for VLM post-training, addressing the real bottleneck of scarce verifiable rewards outside math/code domains.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: six VQA benchmarks (MMBench, SEED-Bench, V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite), open-ended captioning (CapArena), vision-centric classification (ImageNet-1K), and an out-of-modality extension to graph learning (node classification, link prediction).

Thorough ablation suite covering data volume scaling, model size scaling (3B vs 7B), base model family (Qwen2.5-VL vs Gemma3-4B), task difficulty scaling, and task combination, which yields genuinely useful design principles (e.g., task difficulty must match model capacity, naive multi-task reward combination is not additive).
Inclusion of an oracle baseline (Golden-3B trained with ground-truth downstream rewards) contextualizes how much of the achievable gain SSL4RL captures without any labeled data.

Reasonable transparency: reward formulations, prompts, hyperparameters, and many additional results (reward/entropy/response-length curves, attention-map visualizations, qualitative examples) are provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility along with a promise to release code.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea of using pretext tasks (e.g., jigsaw) as RLVR signals is already established in cited concurrent/prior work (Jigsaw-R1, Spatial-SSRL); this paper's contribution is largely a broader empirical study and task unification rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

No control experiment isolating the effect of the SSL task content itself from the generic effect of RL fine-tuning with a structured "think/answer" format and a verifiable binary/discrete reward (e.g., a random or trivial reward baseline). Without this, it is hard to rule out that gains partly stem from general RL-induced structured reasoning rather than the specific SSL semantics.

Potential train/benchmark overlap: the data-volume scaling ablation (Appendix E) explicitly trains SSL4RL-Position on images drawn from MMBench and SEED-Bench and then evaluates on the same benchmarks; it is unclear whether the main results (Section 4.1/Table 1) also train on images sourced from these evaluation benchmarks, raising concerns about image-level leakage inflating reported gains.

Several explanatory claims (e.g., rotation prediction as "anti-commonsense learning" sharpening relational reasoning, sub-task specific causal stories for why Position aids logical reasoning) are speculative narratives not directly tested with targeted controlled experiments.

No reported variance over multiple seeds/runs despite RL training being known to be noisy; all results are single-run point estimates, making it difficult to assess the statistical reliability of reported differences, some of which are small (e.g., 7B gains of ~1%).

The open-ended captioning evaluation shows some unusual results (e.g., base model GPT-Score of exactly 0.00) that are not explained, and the min-max normalization procedure used for CapArena scores is not fully detailed, making it hard to interpret absolute magnitudes.

The vision-centric ImageNet evaluation compares only the VLM before/after SSL4RL rather than against specialist vision classifiers or other representative baselines, so the claim about closing the gap with "specialist vision models" from the introduction is not directly substantiated by the experiments shown.
